description.short: The world's first black tea in history — smoked over pine wood embers with a resinous, smoky aroma
description.overview: Regarded as the ancestor of all black (red) teas in the world. It was invented in Tongmu village as a method to quickly dry tea leaves over an open pine fire when time was short, accidentally giving birth to an entirely new category of tea.
description.leaf: Dark brown, twisted leaves, often displaying a subtle resinous sheen
description.aroma: Smoky, resinous pine wood, with undertones of dried fruits and longan
description.taste: Smoky, gently sweet, full-bodied with a mellow texture
description.aftertaste: Long and persistent with lingering warm smoky notes
description.processing: Plucking → withering over pine fire → rolling → full oxidation → drying and smoking with smoldering pine wood smoke in specialized multi-story smokehouses (Qinglou)

history.origin: According to legend, passing soldiers occupied a tea workshop in Tongmu, delaying the processing of fresh leaves. To salvage the crop, tea makers accelerated drying over open fires fueled by local pine wood — unintentionally creating the world's first black tea.
history.development: This occurred around the 17th century; the tea quickly gained immense popularity in Europe through the East India Company trade and became one of the first Chinese teas widely celebrated in the West.
history.modern: The name 'Lapsang Souchong', widely recognized in the West, is a dialect transliteration; today many imitations exist, but authentic Zhengshan Xiaozhong is produced exclusively within the protected Tongmu reserve.
interestingFacts: Regarded as the first black (fully oxidized) tea in human history — all subsequent black teas worldwide trace their technological lineage back to this innovation.
Traditional smoking workshops (Qinglou) in Tongmu are multi-story wooden buildings where tea leaves are spread on upper floors while pine wood embers smolder on the ground floor below.
